To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in the case of a patient presenting with an upper airway infection, the following should be taken into account for the decision to administer antibiotics: (1) the individual situation, (2) the epidemiological situation, (3) the possible pathogens and their antibiotic resistance, (4) the side effects and (5) the costs.

in most cases the patient's symptoms will subside without antibiotics and that the physician must consider the clinical picture and the individual and epidemiologic situation, the possible pathogen and its resistance, the side effects, and costs of antibiotics before prescribing them.
in the case of an acute airway infection, in the absence of concomittant symptoms or circumstances, no antibiotic is needed, but symptomatic treatment.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in most cases of acute airway infections antibiotics are not indicated.
antibiotics are indicated in the following cases: 1. acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, 2. acute otitis media, 3. acute tonsillitis, 4. acute epiglottidis, 5. acute exacerbation of a chronic bronchitis.
in most patients with upper airway infections the use of antibiotics can be avoided and that in those who need antibiotics the use of antibiotics should be restricted to a short course.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have to learn to treat more often without antibiotics.
we have to be careful with antibiotics, that we should use them only when indicated and that we should use only those antibiotics which are indicated.
the physician should be able to distinguish between the "real" and the "perceived" need for an antibiotic therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antibiotics should only be given if the patient's condition has worsened or if the patient is at risk of worsening.
the use of antibiotics in upper airway infections should be reduced as far as possible.
the physician should always be aware of the fact that he is not just prescribing an antibiotic but a drug with a potential risk for the patient and for the society as a whole.
